hits.section: ### S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
hits.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

hits.section: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

hits.section: ### S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem
hits.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

hits.section: ### S16 — A nilpotent kernel is not a zero kernel
hits.text: Under algebraicity of the Künneth components, Jannsen (1992, Corollary 1) identifies the kernel from homological to numerical degree-zero correspondence algebras with the Jacobson radical and proves it nilpotent. This isolates a precise obstruction to obtaining the draft's cohomological semisimplicity from numerical semisimplicity. Nilpotence alone permits a nonzero ideal, so it is not a proof that the two equivalence relations coincide; an additional positivity or equivalence argument must annihilate that kernel. The distinction also prevents treating a numerical projector as a canonical cohomological projector solely because some lift exists.

hits.section: ### S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
hits.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

hits.section: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

hits.section: ### S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem
hits.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

hits.section: ### S4 — The written matrix-unit bound is not the string bound
hits.text: The frozen reading has upper bound \(2n-i\), whereas the exponent indexing the successive vectors of a string beginning in degree \(i\) ranges through \(0\leq a\leq n-i\). These are different quantities: \(2n-i\) is the top cohomological degree, while \(n-i\) counts applications of the degree-two operator. The inserted \(\pi_{i+2\alpha,\alpha}\) makes that distinction especially pertinent, but neither the expected dimension nor the matrix-unit multiplication authorizes changing the visible bound; an edition should retain it and place the normalized comparison here.

hits.text: The criterion in scan 48 replaces a particular Lefschetz inverse by the existence of some algebraic isomorphism between complementary degrees, together with rationality of characteristic polynomials. Neither requirement mentions the chosen ample class, so—once the criterion's hypotheses hold for the fixed theory—the argument applies to another polarization through its own hard Lefschetz isomorphism. Kleiman (1968, §§2.9–2.10) proves this criterion and polarization independence. This reasoning does not itself produce one cycle working for every \(\ell\), identify the draft's undefined \(D_\ell\), or justify removing every parameter in scan 44.

hits.section: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. More generally, the standard rank-\(2n\) symplectic bivector satisfies \(\xi^n=n!\,\mathrm{vol}\), giving the same obstruction for \(n\ge2\). Thus, under the ordinary meaning of the explicitly written exterior algebra and multiplication operator, the integral model does not satisfy the displayed hard-Lefschetz isomorphism in degree 0; rational coefficients, divided powers, or a different lattice would have to be specified in a reconstructed statement. None of those possible repairs is inserted into the transcription.

hits.section: ### R9 — Unpursued implication: identify the cited injective-module results precisely
hits.text: The decomposition and filtration statements have direct counterparts in Matlis (1958, Theorem 2.5, Proposition 3.1, and Theorem 3.10): the last result identifies the successive annihilator quotients with duals of the corresponding graded pieces of the maximal ideal after localization. This supplies a precise reference for the displayed dimension equality without identifying the reused typescript's author or date. In particular, uniqueness here is uniqueness of the isomorphism classes and multiplicities of summands, not a canonical choice of embedded summands; the latter distinction matters when using this decomposition to construct sheaves.

hits.section: ### R10 — Own idea: isolate the adjunction in the injective-sheaf argument
hits.text: Since taking a stalk is exact, the right side is exact contravariantly in \(F\), proving that \(i_{x*}I\) is injective among all \(\mathcal O_X\)-modules. For the particular injective hull \(I=E(k(\mathfrak p))\) used on the page, the distinct geometric step is the identification \(\widetilde I\simeq i_{x*}I\): the displayed filtration reduces it to modules annihilated by powers of \(\mathfrak p\), for which localization is zero when the inverted element belongs to \(\mathfrak p\) and is an isomorphism when it does not. This separates the general adjunction argument from the noetherian algebra needed to establish that identification.

hits.section: ### R11 — Reading question: recover the hypotheses preceding the local surface fragment
hits.text: The corresponding published passage assumes a complete normal two-dimensional local ring with algebraically closed residue field, a regular resolution, and an isomorphism away from the closed point (Grothendieck, 1968, §8.4, pp. 148–149). These hypotheses belong to the external comparison and must not be supplied as missing manuscript text. They delimit the setting in which the quotient identified on the supplied sheet is to be compared with the discriminant group in R4.

hits.section: ### R12 — Unproved claim: a later compatibility check remains explicitly unfinished
hits.text: The published continuation asks for compatibility between the discriminant pairing and the cohomological construction, and Remark 8.5 acknowledges that this verification has not been carried out (Grothendieck, 1968, pp. 150–151). Thus the elementary matrix calculation in R4 does not by itself establish that compatibility. A reconstruction must compare the cycle class, Kummer boundary, cup product, and local trace maps with their signs, rather than merely exhibit two perfect pairings on abstractly isomorphic finite groups.

hits.section: ### S7 — Hard Lefschetz supplies linear inverses, not their cycles
hits.text: Deligne (1980, Theorem 4.1.1) proves hard Lefschetz for an ample class on a smooth projective variety over an algebraically closed field, with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients and \(\ell\) different from the characteristic: \(L^{n-i}:H^i\to H^{2n-i}\) is an isomorphism. Applied to the draft, this settles the existence of the indicated cohomological inverses in that setting, while the additional demand that an inverse arise from a rational algebraic correspondence remains a separate assertion. Keeping these two steps explicit also prevents the later theorem from concealing the integral obstruction in scan 14, where the coefficient ring is \(\mathbb Z\).

hits.section: ### S12 — Polarization independence is different from theory independence
hits.text: The criterion in scan 48 replaces a particular Lefschetz inverse by the existence of some algebraic isomorphism between complementary degrees, together with rationality of characteristic polynomials. Neither requirement mentions the chosen ample class, so—once the criterion's hypotheses hold for the fixed theory—the argument applies to another polarization through its own hard Lefschetz isomorphism. Kleiman (1968, §§2.9–2.10) proves this criterion and polarization independence. This reasoning does not itself produce one cycle working for every \(\ell\), identify the draft's undefined \(D_\ell\), or justify removing every parameter in scan 44.

hits.section: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

hits.section: ### S17 — Finite-field Künneth projectors illustrate a narrower later result
hits.text: For smooth projective varieties over finite fields, Katz and Messing (1974, Theorem 2) construct rational algebraic Künneth projectors as rational combinations of graphs of Frobenius iterates, compatibly with the cohomology theories in their hypotheses. Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

The planned proof compares the trace-defined Dedekind different and the Kähler different for discrete valuation rings. The outline points to a dévissage and local complete-intersection lemmas, whose exact references are internal and cannot be resolved from this page alone.

The proposed appendix states invariance of finite étale algebras under a nilpotent thickening A→A/I and points to S. G. A. A proof would establish both lifting of objects and unique lifting of morphisms, yielding an equivalence of categories rather than only a bijection on isomorphism classes.

The finite p-group is presented as an extension of a Cartier dual infinitesimal group by the group associated with t_A. This can be compared directly with the earlier Hodge–de Rham extension, but compatibility of extension classes is not established on this sheet.

The draft claims integrality of the root pairings and sketches a route through indivisibility of each root in the lattice. It in turn invokes membership in a fundamental root system. The logical dependence of existence of such a system on the stated axioms needs to be checked to avoid using integrality inside its own proof.

Make a dependency diagram for the axioms: root-set symmetry, invariant positive form, uniqueness of reflection, existence of a fundamental system, primitivity, and integral coroot pairing. Then examine which steps survive if the root lattice is replaced by an intermediate lattice, since the manuscript’s two presentations may encode different lattice conventions.

hits.section: ### R16 — Unproved claim: trace duality needs its own assumptions
hits.text: The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

hits.section: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. More generally, the standard rank-\(2n\) symplectic bivector satisfies \(\xi^n=n!\,\mathrm{vol}\), giving the same obstruction for \(n\ge2\). Thus, under the ordinary meaning of the explicitly written exterior algebra and multiplication operator, the integral model does not satisfy the displayed hard-Lefschetz isomorphism in degree 0; rational coefficients, divided powers, or a different lattice would have to be specified in a reconstructed statement. None of those possible repairs is inserted into the transcription.

hits.section: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

hits.section: ### S6 — Intrinsic projectors still require the graded-ring hypotheses
hits.text: Kleiman's (1968, §3.15) corresponding uniqueness lemma uses the degree-zero center and annihilators. In the manuscript, the relevant data are the entire graded ring, orthogonal idempotents summing to one, the decomposition by their degree differences, and inverse identities between complementary pieces. Thus an intrinsic characterization within that structure should not be restated as recovery from an ungraded element \(L\), nor does the published typography settle the uncertain font of the manuscript's center symbol. The useful comparison is the logical role of each hypothesis, particularly the inverse identity that turns an annihilator of a graded component into an annihilator of its projector.

hits.section: ### S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
hits.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

hits.section: ### S16 — A nilpotent kernel is not a zero kernel
hits.text: Under algebraicity of the Künneth components, Jannsen (1992, Corollary 1) identifies the kernel from homological to numerical degree-zero correspondence algebras with the Jacobson radical and proves it nilpotent. This isolates a precise obstruction to obtaining the draft's cohomological semisimplicity from numerical semisimplicity. Nilpotence alone permits a nonzero ideal, so it is not a proof that the two equivalence relations coincide; an additional positivity or equivalence argument must annihilate that kernel. The distinction also prevents treating a numerical projector as a canonical cohomological projector solely because some lift exists.

hits.section: ### S17 — Finite-field Künneth projectors illustrate a narrower later result
hits.text: For smooth projective varieties over finite fields, Katz and Messing (1974, Theorem 2) construct rational algebraic Künneth projectors as rational combinations of graphs of Frobenius iterates, compatibly with the cohomology theories in their hypotheses. Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

hits.section: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. More generally, the standard rank-\(2n\) symplectic bivector satisfies \(\xi^n=n!\,\mathrm{vol}\), giving the same obstruction for \(n\ge2\). Thus, under the ordinary meaning of the explicitly written exterior algebra and multiplication operator, the integral model does not satisfy the displayed hard-Lefschetz isomorphism in degree 0; rational coefficients, divided powers, or a different lattice would have to be specified in a reconstructed statement. hits.section: ### R16 — Unproved claim: trace duality needs its own assumptions

The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

hits.text: If this is read without further ambient hypotheses, let \(A=k[t]\) and \(B=A\times A/(t)\), with the diagonal \(A\)-algebra structure; then \(B\) is finite and its fibre at every maximal ideal is either \(k(\mathfrak m)\) or \(k(\mathfrak m)\times k(\mathfrak m)\), hence is finite étale. But \(B\simeq A\oplus A/(t)\) as an \(A\)-module is not flat, since multiplication by \(t\) kills a nonzero element, so \(B/A\) is not étale. Accordingly, the proposed equivalence needs the hypotheses of the referenced text to supply flatness or a condition that forces it; the counterexample does not decide whether those hypotheses were already in force. Using a product with the \(A\)-factor ensures that every fibre is nonempty, so this objection is not an artefact of allowing the zero algebra as an empty cover.

hits.section: ### S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem
hits.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

hits.section: ### F15 — Cote 47, scan 9, question about torsion
hits.text: A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms. These additional hypotheses and the distinction between rational identities and integral lifts prevent the manuscript’s local heuristic from being treated as a general integral-transform theorem.

hits.section: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. More generally, the standard rank-\(2n\) symplectic bivector satisfies \(\xi^n=n!\,\mathrm{vol}\), giving the same obstruction for \(n\ge2\). Thus, under the ordinary meaning of the explicitly written exterior algebra and multiplication operator, the integral model does not satisfy the displayed hard-Lefschetz isomorphism in degree 0; rational coefficients, divided powers, or a different lattice would have to be specified in a reconstructed statement. None of those possible repairs is inserted into the transcription.

hits.section: ### R16 — Unproved claim: trace duality needs its own assumptions
hits.text: The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

The essential proof obligation is convergence with only finitely many relevant terms in each total degree, followed by coherence of the ordinary Ext modules. In the finite-injective-dimension version of case (b), truncating the first argument reduces each fixed output degree to case (a), as in Tag 0G4H, Lemma 47.15.2; one must still justify how the page's uniform sheaf-Ext bound supplies the needed local truncation estimate. hits.section: ### R22 — Own idea: test the finite-fibre criterion without hidden flatness
hits.text: If this is read without further ambient hypotheses, let \(A=k[t]\) and \(B=A\times A/(t)\), with the diagonal \(A\)-algebra structure; then \(B\) is finite and its fibre at every maximal ideal is either \(k(\mathfrak m)\) or \(k(\mathfrak m)\times k(\mathfrak m)\), hence is finite étale. But \(B\simeq A\oplus A/(t)\) as an \(A\)-module is not flat, since multiplication by \(t\) kills a nonzero element, so \(B/A\) is not étale. Accordingly, the proposed equivalence needs the hypotheses of the referenced text to supply flatness or a condition that forces it; the counterexample does not decide whether those hypotheses were already in force. Using a product with the \(A\)-factor ensures that every fibre is nonempty, so this objection is not an artefact of allowing the zero algebra as an empty cover.

hits.section: ### S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem
hits.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

hits.section: ### F15 — Cote 47, scan 9, question about torsion
hits.text: A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms. These additional hypotheses and the distinction between rational identities and integral lifts prevent the manuscript’s local heuristic from being treated as a general integral-transform theorem.

hits.text: The criterion in scan 48 replaces a particular Lefschetz inverse by the existence of some algebraic isomorphism between complementary degrees, together with rationality of characteristic polynomials. Neither requirement mentions the chosen ample class, so—once the criterion's hypotheses hold for the fixed theory—the argument applies to another polarization through its own hard Lefschetz isomorphism. Kleiman (1968, §§2.9–2.10) proves this criterion and polarization independence. This reasoning does not itself produce one cycle working for every \(\ell\), identify the draft's undefined \(D_\ell\), or justify removing every parameter in scan 44.

hits.section: ### R17 — Unpursued implication: the proposed nilpotent appendix is a categorical statement
hits.text: Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). For the proposed appendix, one must prove both lifting of finite étale algebras and unique lifting of their morphisms; existence of lifted defining equations alone proves neither the full equivalence nor its functoriality. The statement concerns the category of covers, and is compatible with the underlying scheme retaining its nilpotent structure.

hits.section: ### S7 — Hard Lefschetz supplies linear inverses, not their cycles
hits.text: Deligne (1980, Theorem 4.1.1) proves hard Lefschetz for an ample class on a smooth projective variety over an algebraically closed field, with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients and \(\ell\) different from the characteristic: \(L^{n-i}:H^i\to H^{2n-i}\) is an isomorphism. hits.section: ### S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem
hits.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

hits.section: ### S16 — A nilpotent kernel is not a zero kernel
hits.text: Under algebraicity of the Künneth components, Jannsen (1992, Corollary 1) identifies the kernel from homological to numerical degree-zero correspondence algebras with the Jacobson radical and proves it nilpotent. This isolates a precise obstruction to obtaining the draft's cohomological semisimplicity from numerical semisimplicity. Nilpotence alone permits a nonzero ideal, so it is not a proof that the two equivalence relations coincide; an additional positivity or equivalence argument must annihilate that kernel. The distinction also prevents treating a numerical projector as a canonical cohomological projector solely because some lift exists.

hits.section: ### S17 — Finite-field Künneth projectors illustrate a narrower later result
hits.text: For smooth projective varieties over finite fields, Katz and Messing (1974, Theorem 2) construct rational algebraic Künneth projectors as rational combinations of graphs of Frobenius iterates, compatibly with the cohomology theories in their hypotheses. Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

hits.section: ## Integral models, local duality, and reused typescripts
hits.text: The following items distinguish calculations made directly from the frozen pages from external comparisons made only after the transcription was frozen. Their conclusions are conditional wherever a normalization or an antecedent hypothesis is not supplied on the surviving sheet; no mathematical correction is inserted into the transcription.

hits.section: ### R2 — Own idea: contraction and the unweighted lowering operator
hits.text: Choose the contraction convention \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{std}}=\sum_j\iota_{f_j^\vee}\iota_{e_j^\vee}\) in the rank-four example of R1; then \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{std}}L(1)=2\), whereas the endpoint identity \(\Lambda L=1-\sum_{j\ge n}\pi_{j,0}\) acts as 1 on degree 0. Over a characteristic-zero field, a primitive vector of degree \(i\) in an ordinary Lefschetz string satisfies \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{std}}(L^j p)=j(n-i-j+1)L^{j-1}p\), while an unweighted inverse along the same string sends \(L^j p\) to \(L^{j-1}p\). These are different operators even after rationalizing the integral model, so rationalization by itself does not settle the identification made on scan 14. The precise definition of contraction and any normalization outside the supplied pages must be checked before attributing a finished theorem to this draft.

hits.section: ### R4 — Own idea: an explicit discriminant pairing
hits.text: Replacing \(x\) or \(y\) by a representative differing by a column combination of \(Q\) changes the value by an integer, and the dual-lattice description proves that this pairing is perfect. In the rank-one case \(Q=(-m)\), it becomes \(b_Q(\bar a,\bar b)=-ab/m\pmod{\mathbb Z}\) on \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\), making both the determinant and the sign convention visible. This supplies the linear-algebra part of the claim on the page; identifying the geometric Néron–Severi quotient with \(D_Q\) still depends on the preceding geometric hypotheses.

hits.section: ### R6 — Own idea: a finite-field obstruction to the polynomial argument
hits.text: Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. Nevertheless, after extending scalars to an algebraic closure there are elements with three distinct coordinates, so the Vandermonde discriminant polynomial is not the zero polynomial. Thus passage to the algebraic closure proves polynomial nonvanishing without proving existence of a \(k\)-rational point of its nonvanishing locus. This is a conditional objection to the argument as preserved on this sheet, because an infinitude hypothesis may have been supplied in the antecedent text that is not present here.

hits.section: ### R9 — Unpursued implication: identify the cited injective-module results precisely
hits.text: The decomposition and filtration statements have direct counterparts in Matlis (1958, Theorem 2.5, Proposition 3.1, and Theorem 3.10): the last result identifies the successive annihilator quotients with duals of the corresponding graded pieces of the maximal ideal after localization. This supplies a precise reference for the displayed dimension equality without identifying the reused typescript's author or date. In particular, uniqueness here is uniqueness of the isomorphism classes and multiplicities of summands, not a canonical choice of embedded summands; the latter distinction matters when using this decomposition to construct sheaves.

These hypotheses belong to the external comparison and must not be supplied as missing manuscript text. They delimit the setting in which the quotient identified on the supplied sheet is to be compared with the discriminant group in R4.

hits.section: ### R16 — Unproved claim: trace duality needs its own assumptions
hits.text: The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

hits.section: ### R17 — Unpursued implication: the proposed nilpotent appendix is a categorical statement
hits.text: Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). For the proposed appendix, one must prove both lifting of finite étale algebras and unique lifting of their morphisms; existence of lifted defining equations alone proves neither the full equivalence nor its functoriality. The statement concerns the category of covers, and is compatible with the underlying scheme retaining its nilpotent structure.

hits.text: For coherent cohomology, case (a) has a precise current counterpart: a bounded-above first argument and bounded-below second argument give coherent internal derived Hom on a locally noetherian scheme (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0D0C, Lemma 36.11.5). The essential proof obligation is convergence with only finitely many relevant terms in each total degree, followed by coherence of the ordinary Ext modules. In the finite-injective-dimension version of case (b), truncating the first argument reduces each fixed output degree to case (a), as in Tag 0G4H, Lemma 47.15.2; one must still justify how the page's uniform sheaf-Ext bound supplies the needed local truncation estimate. The quasi-coherent variant and the exact scope of that uniform bound should be checked separately rather than inferred from the coherent statement alone.

hits.section: ### S7 — Hard Lefschetz supplies linear inverses, not their cycles
hits.text: Deligne (1980, Theorem 4.1.1) proves hard Lefschetz for an ample class on a smooth projective variety over an algebraically closed field, with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients and \(\ell\) different from the characteristic: \(L^{n-i}:H^i\to H^{2n-i}\) is an isomorphism. Applied to the draft, this settles the existence of the indicated cohomological inverses in that setting, while the additional demand that an inverse arise from a rational algebraic correspondence remains a separate assertion. Keeping these two steps explicit also prevents the later theorem from concealing the integral obstruction in scan 14, where the coefficient ring is \(\mathbb Z\).

hits.section: ### S12 — Polarization independence is different from theory independence
hits.text: The criterion in scan 48 replaces a particular Lefschetz inverse by the existence of some algebraic isomorphism between complementary degrees, together with rationality of characteristic polynomials. Neither requirement mentions the chosen ample class, so—once the criterion's hypotheses hold for the fixed theory—the argument applies to another polarization through its own hard Lefschetz isomorphism. Kleiman (1968, §§2.9–2.10) proves this criterion and polarization independence. This reasoning does not itself produce one cycle working for every \(\ell\), identify the draft's undefined \(D_\ell\), or justify removing every parameter in scan 44.

hits.section: ### S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
hits.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

hits.section: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

hits.section: ### S16 — A nilpotent kernel is not a zero kernel
hits.text: Under algebraicity of the Künneth components, Jannsen (1992, Corollary 1) identifies the kernel from homological to numerical degree-zero correspondence algebras with the Jacobson radical and proves it nilpotent. This isolates a precise obstruction to obtaining the draft's cohomological semisimplicity from numerical semisimplicity. Nilpotence alone permits a nonzero ideal, so it is not a proof that the two equivalence relations coincide; an additional positivity or equivalence argument must annihilate that kernel. The distinction also prevents treating a numerical projector as a canonical cohomological projector solely because some lift exists.

hits.section: ### S18 — Read the low-dimensional list as a dated list
hits.text: Kleiman (1968, §§2A9–2A10, 3.4) supplies proofs of the listed positive assertions on surfaces and characteristic-zero varieties of dimension at most four. The nearby negative assertions belong to the letter's discussion and should not be converted into blanket claims about present knowledge, especially while draft \(B\) and \(D\) remain undefined here. Likewise, the written 1966 date on scan 48 and 1967 date on scan 44 should remain separate documentary facts rather than being silently harmonized to create a chronology. The precise mathematical bottleneck identified in scan 47 is the critical condition on a threefold times a hyperplane surface, which the earlier product reduction connects to its strong Lefschetz condition.

hits.section: ### R6 — Own idea: a finite-field obstruction to the polynomial argument
hits.text: Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. Nevertheless, after extending scalars to an algebraic closure there are elements with three distinct coordinates, so the Vandermonde discriminant polynomial is not the zero polynomial. Thus passage to the algebraic closure proves polynomial nonvanishing without proving existence of a \(k\)-rational point of its nonvanishing locus. This is a conditional objection to the argument as preserved on this sheet, because an infinitude hypothesis may have been supplied in the antecedent text that is not present here.

hits.section: ### R7 — Reading question: the typed word “homogènes”
hits.text: The typescript visibly says “homogènes”, although no grading has been introduced on this surviving page. Reading it as a claim about principal or monogenic maximal ideals would be a mathematical emendation, and even that emendation would need a field-size qualification: in \(\mathbb F_2^3\), every maximal ideal is generated by an idempotent while the algebra is not monogenic, as in R6. The appropriate research task is to locate the referenced proposition and its hypotheses, then compare its terminology with the exact typed wording retained here.

hits.section: ### R22 — Own idea: test the finite-fibre criterion without hidden flatness
hits.text: If this is read without further ambient hypotheses, let \(A=k[t]\) and \(B=A\times A/(t)\), with the diagonal \(A\)-algebra structure; then \(B\) is finite and its fibre at every maximal ideal is either \(k(\mathfrak m)\) or \(k(\mathfrak m)\times k(\mathfrak m)\), hence is finite étale. But \(B\simeq A\oplus A/(t)\) as an \(A\)-module is not flat, since multiplication by \(t\) kills a nonzero element, so \(B/A\) is not étale. Accordingly, the proposed equivalence needs the hypotheses of the referenced text to supply flatness or a condition that forces it; the counterexample does not decide whether those hypotheses were already in force. Using a product with the \(A\)-factor ensures that every fibre is nonempty, so this objection is not an artefact of allowing the zero algebra as an empty cover.

hits.section: ### R22 — Own idea: test the finite-fibre criterion without hidden flatness
hits.text: If this is read without further ambient hypotheses, let \(A=k[t]\) and \(B=A\times A/(t)\), with the diagonal \(A\)-algebra structure; then \(B\) is finite and its fibre at every maximal ideal is either \(k(\mathfrak m)\) or \(k(\mathfrak m)\times k(\mathfrak m)\), hence is finite étale. But \(B\simeq A\oplus A/(t)\) as an \(A\)-module is not flat, since multiplication by \(t\) kills a nonzero element, so \(B/A\) is not étale. Accordingly, the proposed equivalence needs the hypotheses of the referenced text to supply flatness or a condition that forces it; the counterexample does not decide whether those hypotheses were already in force. Using a product with the \(A\)-factor ensures that every fibre is nonempty, so this objection is not an artefact of allowing the zero algebra as an empty cover.

hits.text: A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms. These additional hypotheses and the distinction between rational identities and integral lifts prevent the manuscript’s local heuristic from being treated as a general integral-transform theorem.

hits.section: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. More generally, the standard rank-\(2n\) symplectic bivector satisfies \(\xi^n=n!\,\mathrm{vol}\), giving the same obstruction for \(n\ge2\). Thus, under the ordinary meaning of the explicitly written exterior algebra and multiplication operator, the integral model does not satisfy the displayed hard-Lefschetz isomorphism in degree 0; rational coefficients, divided powers, or a different lattice would have to be specified in a reconstructed statement. None of those possible repairs is inserted into the transcription.

hits.section: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

Autre question de terminologie : le Congrès avait adopté d'enthousiasme une belle terminologie symétrique : ``poids'', ``poids radiciels'', ``copoids'', ``copoids radiciels''. Le malheur est qu'avec la définition adoptée, un ``copoids radiciel'' \uline{n'est pas} nécessairement un ``copoids'', ce qui est grammaticalement intolérable. Le rédacteur voit trois solutions possibles :

1) Prendre une autre terminologie pour ``poids radiciels'' et ``copoids radiciels'' ; c'est la solution adoptée dans la rédaction, qui dit respectivement ``vocables'' et ``covocables'', (dactylo, attention, ce n'est \uline{pas} ``convocables''!). Le rédacteur ne tient pas spécialement à ces termes ; on pourrait aussi dire ``noeuds'' et ``conoeuds'' bien que ce dernier mot ait l'air un peu ... ce que vous pensez.

2) On ne peut naturellement changer le sens reçu de ``racines'' et ``poids'' ; mais ``copoids'' est beaucoup plus récent, (Chevalley, je crois), et pas encore très répandu ; on pourrait donc intervertir les sens de ``copoids'' et ``copoids radiciels'', les poids étant donc associés aux copoids radiciels, (et non plus aux copoids), et les copoids radiciels étant engendrés par les coracines, (ce qui est assez satisfaisant).

3) N'utiliser aucune terminologie pour ``poids radiciels'' et ``copoids radiciels'' ; l'expérience, (tout au moins dans la présente rédaction), montre qu'on s'en sert en fait très peu et qu'on s'en passe fort bien.

hits.text: A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms. hits.section: ### S9 — Hyperplane reduction has product hypotheses and quantifiers
hits.text: The displayed identity \(\Lambda_Y=\varphi^*\Lambda_X^2\varphi_*\) has degree \(-2\), since restriction has degree zero and the Gysin map raises degree by two, so it transports algebraicity downward when \(\Lambda_X\) is already algebraic. Reversing that argument in the source requires critical-degree algebraicity on a self-product or an adjacent hyperplane product; Kleiman (1968, §§2.12–2.14) proves the corresponding hyperplane and flag implications. Consequently the letter's \(A(k)=C(k)\) concerns conditions quantified over all relevant varieties, not an implication from the weak condition on a single \(X\) to its own strong condition. Grothendieck (1969, §3) likewise distinguishes \(B(X)\Rightarrow A(X)\) from \(A(X\times X)\Rightarrow B(X)\).

hits.section: ### S10 — The weak variants need a separate degree audit
hits.text: The text mixes \(i\), \(j\), doubled inequalities, and \(H^i\) versus \(H^{j+2}\), so the proposed equivalences should not be quoted as a fully settled indexed statement. An editorial reconstruction can first record that restriction preserves cohomological degree, the Gysin map raises it by two, and \(L=\varphi_*\varphi^*\); the two visible factorizations then have total degree four and two respectively. Only after specifying whether an index measures codimension or cohomological degree can one formulate consistent critical ranges. That reconstruction would be a new explanatory statement, while the diplomatic transcription continues to preserve the written ranges and overwritten conclusion.

hits.text: Dualizing the Hodge-line identification gives \(\det\operatorname{Lie}A\simeq\det\operatorname{Lie}B\), without a principal polarization or an identification of the full Lie bundles. His Lemma 1.2.5 also identifies the Poincaré direct image with the zero-section pushforward of this inverse Hodge line, shifted by \(-g\); this preserves canonicity without choosing a trivialization.

hits.section: ### F6 — Cote 47, scan 7, admitted Lemma 2 and following support argument
hits.text: The attributed statement is explicitly present in Mumford (1970, §8(vii), p. 76): a nontrivial algebraically trivial line bundle on an abelian variety has vanishing cohomology in every degree. Together with base change, it removes the Poincaré direct image away from the zero section. It does not alone determine the scheme-theoretic structure along that section, the surviving cohomological degree, the determinant twist, or the specific comparison map constructed at the bottom of the page.

hits.section: ### F7 — Cote 47, scan 8, first paragraph and unfinished verification
hits.text: **Editorial proof plan:** the direct image of the Poincaré line bundle is perfect, and the zero-section pushforward is perfect because that section is a regular immersion, so the cone of the proposed comparison is perfect. Vanishing of all its derived residue-field fibres then proves that the cone vanishes, by the local perfect-complex criterion (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0DJT and 0G99). The remaining task is to show that the particular map induces the required isomorphisms at the unit, not merely that the two sides have equal cohomology dimensions. **Confidence: high**, because the finite-complex criterion is established and isolates exactly the manuscript’s unfinished step.

hits.section: ### F15 — Cote 47, scan 9, question about torsion
hits.text: A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms. These additional hypotheses and the distinction between rational identities and integral lifts prevent the manuscript’s local heuristic from being treated as a general integral-transform theorem.

The claim is that a subring containing every graded projector inherits the homogeneous decomposition of the endomorphism ring. A proof has to use the finiteness of the grading to ensure that the displayed sums remain algebraic sums inside the subring, and then check multiplication of the components.

The degree-combination mark looks like a short dash or an incomplete plus. Additive degree composition suggests a plus, but that mathematical expectation has not been substituted for the visible mark.

The written base-case insertion appears to say that all projectors except π_n are known when i=n−1; this does not immediately match the neighbouring interval statement. The indices should be rechecked against the next page and the ink, with any mathematical repair confined to the notes.

This is the key uniqueness step: in a commutative ring an idempotent is determined by its annihilator, since its complementary principal ideal records the same decomposition. The argument also requires that the relevant projectors lie in the centre of E^0, as established on the preceding sheet.

The module argument is recast internally in the graded ring using two homogeneous elements that are mutual inverses on the specified projector blocks. The displayed calculation proves the first annihilator implication and refers to the second by symmetry; one should check that the degree-zero element commutes with the projectors in precisely the manner already established.

The induction is rewritten several times and again has a potentially delicate terminal index. Compare this formulation with the corresponding insertion on scan5 before deciding whether the text has an indexing slip or a different convention for what is already known.

Check the two proposed expressions for q on each primitive summand before using q as a complementary projector. In particular, the final summand’s visible index looks unprimed although α′ is the summation variable; a proof may require a different expression, but that would be an editorial reconstruction.

The two displayed projector formulae give an explicit construction from L, chosen inverse operators and projectors already obtained by induction. Comparing different choices of the inverse operators could show directly that the resulting primitive projectors are independent of those choices.

Reduce the remaining membership of Λ to its action on a single primitive string and then express each nonzero restriction using the operators already in the ring. Keep the index change from j in (6.11) to i in the final sentence visible while reconstructing that argument.

The eight relations are announced as an intrinsic uniqueness characterisation of Λ and the primitive projectors in terms of L and the coarse grading projectors. A proof must establish both that the constructed operators satisfy every surviving relation and that any solution is unique; the remark supplies the system but not those two verifications.

The surviving multiplication rule has the form of matrix units indexed by primitive degree and string position. If the asserted nonzero ranges and linear independence hold, it suggests a product of full matrix algebras, but those conditions must be proved before making that identification.

The author directs that the generators and their multiplication be placed in the earlier exposition. This is an editorial instruction about the manuscript’s organisation, not a missing formula that may be supplied by the transcriber.

The corollary asserts uniqueness of the homomorphism subject to preservation of both L and the grading projectors. The result depends on the preceding proposition and on the uniqueness of the projector family from the graded ring; the added integer 2n≥0 supplies an explicit parameter for that assertion.

The author asks whether the image of L alone determines at most one homomorphism, then answers negatively on the same page. The n=1 example and the final sentence explicitly insist that L and the π_i must be prescribed together; this should not be catalogued as a question left unanswered by the manuscript.

The author claims symmetry after reversing degrees and passing to the opposite ring, and proposes a separate “principe de dualité” section. A proof should specify the transformed grading and multiplication convention and verify that the defining identities survive both reversals.

Test the duality principle and the proposed converse in the smallest product-of-matrix-algebras models suggested by scan15, allowing different scalars on the primitive strings. This may separate failure of invertibility on one string from the weaker fact that the longest power is nonzero.

**Editorial confidence:** medium. A nonzero highest power detects only some components unless additional hypotheses force all required maps to be invertible; the promised later hypotheses may supply exactly that restriction.

This reused typescript is a separate discussion of Picard and Néron–Severi groups, not the continuation of the handwritten Lefschetz paragraph. Its hypotheses begin on an absent preceding typescript page; the extension and rational-point descriptions must be interpreted with that limitation.

The typescript says that resolution independence of the symmetric discriminant pairing is easy to verify but gives no verification here. A proof would compare the intersection lattices under a common refinement and explain why the induced finite pairing is unchanged.

The explicit degree-two-generated algebra has the four written relations and basis groups of sizes1,2,2,1. It claims that equality of the top cubes does not ensure the Lefschetz property. The computation is not carried out here; scan20 contains related scratch relations that should be compared after the transcription is frozen.
**Editorial confidence:** high. The entire conclusion is underlined; superscripts carry visible hatching.

The author separates the divisible part of the cohomological Brauer group from the finite quotient. Kummer and the earlier exact sequence identify that quotient with the torsion of third l-adic cohomology; the final paragraph begins a duality argument that continues off-page.

The handwritten insertion par passage à la limite indicates the intended bridge from finite-coefficient duality to the stated l-adic consequence. The citation is transcribed with its visible extra A and barred/underlined Roman numeral; later bibliographic research should keep that literal form distinct from any corrected identification.

The proposed special case is constructed from an isotropic line in the enlarged quadratic space and a nondegenerate alternating map into that line. A proof must make the assumptions on the field, characteristic, dimension, and nondegeneracy of Q explicit; the deleted discussion may have been addressing precisely these restrictions.

The “to appear” entry for Shatz can help identify the provenance and approximate preparation date of this isolated bibliography page. The printed folio 45 and handwritten 27 should be kept distinct; the page does not itself show how the bibliography relates to the surrounding handwritten Hodge-algebra sheets.

In a chosen basis, form the matrix of χ′ on ∧²V and the tensor-square matrix associated with the bivector, then compute u and the cyclic subspaces generated by ξ and that bivector. Comparing dimensions four, six, and eight would directly test the proposed threshold and distinguish an infinite set-theoretic orbit from large cyclic linear span.

The exceptional middle primitive quotient is identified with a kernel of the push-forward. One can investigate whether this identification is canonical under the choices implicit in the primitive decompositions; the written kernel direct sum has a possible i/j mismatch that must remain a reading issue.

The second reader enlarged the narrow mark and compared its broad triangular head and broken tail. Both readers found the origin uncertain; the shape is represented graphically so that this visible feature is not silently lost, without asserting that it was drawn deliberately.

The push-forward is described on the primitive decomposition and used to identify its kernel with E^{n−1}(Y) and its image with Im L_X. A rigorous reconstruction should check the decomposition map and the exceptional summand; overwritten earlier kernel formulas show that the argument was being revised.

The page begins a classification of quasi-coherent sheaves that are injective among all O_X-modules as direct sums of point-supported injective-hull sheaves. The statement breaks off at the bottom, so its completion and proof must be located before treating the printed conditions as the entire proposition.

The first simple intertwining identities and their attempted verification are enclosed and crossed out. They must not be quoted as surviving conclusions; the lower formulas introduce projector corrections that appear to replace them.

The decomposition is explicitly attributed to Matlis, with a printed journal reference, rather than presented as a new assertion of the manuscript author. Its uniqueness language should be checked against that source after transcription freeze; no canonical choice of summands is specified on this page.

The page reduces C(X), conditional on C(Y), to algebraicity of a natural left inverse to restriction in degrees at most n−1. A proof should track the dependence of that inverse on the polarization and the exact degree cutoff.
The iterated equivalence expresses C(X) through successive adjacent products in a chain of smooth hyperplane sections. The termination/base case of that induction is not supplied on this sheet.

The independent audit enlarged these marks. Both readers confirm the ξ-shaped lower label and the dotted i, which differ from the clear stars elsewhere. In the deleted sum, an open arch favors n over the initial transcription’s 0; that alternative remains local and no mathematical regularization was made.

**Manuscript:** “sufficient to look at what happens in critical dimensions”

The handwritten addition raises a further comparison of an uncertain τ-equivalence with numerical equivalence for 1-cycles; that term must be resolved from the ink before identifying its mathematical content.

A useful reconstruction project would compare candidate singular formulations based on resolutions, intersection cohomology, and correspondences compatible with a resolution, recording precisely which version would make the proposed hypersurface reduction valid. This is an editorial research direction, not a claim that any formulation succeeds.

The proposition claims that Cχ(X) is independent of polarization by characterizing it through algebraic duality isomorphisms and rational characteristic polynomials. The exact χ notation should be cross-checked with the preceding letter before relating this to named standard conjectures.

The expectation is that an algebraic monomorphism admits an algebraic left inverse, hence detects algebraicity of classes. The author gives a hyperplane-section example but says the general case appears to require the Hodge index relation.

The requested proof would construct positivity or a suitable involution on the correspondence algebra and show that its radical vanishes. The final step must explain how semisimplicity supplies the left and right inverses just discussed.

The author explicitly questions whether finite presentation of the module of differentials alone suffices for the proposed definition and results. The different’s base-change behaviour and ramification-locus identification should be tested separately under that weakened assumption.

The construction aims to recover individual primitive-summand projectors by a nested induction, using the kernel N of a Lefschetz power and an inverse map in a lower degree. A finished proof must explicitly identify the kernel, show that its already-constructed summands lie in A, and justify the asserted restriction of the inverse.

As a diagnostic under an unrestricted finite-field reading, test the finite étale algebra F₂×F₂×F₂: a single element has only two possible coordinate values and cannot separate all three factors, so its power-basis discriminant vanishes at every F₂-point. This does not refute a theorem with an unstated infinite-field hypothesis, but it isolates an assumption that the editorial reconstruction must recover.

The final step isolates one primitive-summand projector by subtracting the already available projector onto the strictly higher-power summands from the nested projector onto ξʲH^{k−2j}. A reconstruction should check that both projectors act on the same total cohomology object and that the induction proves the required support, not merely the restriction to Hᵏ.

The criterion is stated for finite-presentation algebras over a noetherian ring and is to be proved using “platitude supérieure”. The reconstruction must specify whether the hats denote completed local rings and track the finite residue extension and descent from completion.

The page characterizes finite étale algebras over connected A by splitting after a faithfully flat base change, with a warning that disconnected bases need a piecewise formulation. A proof should explain local constancy of rank and descent of the finite product algebra structure.

The folder identifies convolution and Fourier transformation on VA as the two linked subjects. The title alone does not specify whether the construction acts on cohomology, cycles, or another invariant; the following leaves must supply the domain and the duality conventions.

The margin proposes replacing an abelian scheme by a flat group scheme and replacing fibrewise algebraic triviality by an explicit multiplicativity identity for the kernel. Proper supports over S and quasi-coherent derived categories are invoked. A complete extension would have to specify the derived pullback/pushforward range and the finiteness conditions under which convolution remains in that range.

A useful continuation would distinguish the existence of the displayed binary isomorphism from coherent compatibility with triple convolution and the unit. One can compare the two pullback-tensor composites on A×A×A×X; agreement would be the concrete extra datum needed for a monoidal formulation. This is a proposed test, not a claim supplied by the manuscript.
**Editorial confidence:** medium. The page supplies a binary kernel relation; associativity and unit coherence require additional equalities that are not checked there.

The source uses a tensor-shaped symbol with subscript S in the external product and a heavily inked star in the convolution. These are retained locally. The next page should clarify the projection labels and whether π denotes the addition map throughout.

The proof makes the multiplicative property of the universal kernel the input that changes convolution into tensor product. This is exactly the datum extracted in the preceding marginal generalization. It would be useful to record which rigidifications make this isomorphism canonical and how its compatibility with repeated addition is established.

Both the dimension hypothesis and the sign are insertions. Their placement indicates that the correction belongs to the stated theorem rather than an unrelated margin calculation. The exact symbol for the symmetry is still a local s/σ ambiguity and must remain distinct from the transposition superscript s on L.

The text has moved from a derived functor calculation to a K-theory inversion theorem. A possible continuation is to test whether the sign arises from a shift by the relative dimension in a stronger composition identity of functors. That stronger statement is a question suggested by the page, not something to add to its transcription or to claim as proved.

A modified transform is asserted to send the ordinary product to convolution, with a corresponding signed class correction on K-theory. Extensive revisions show an attempt to get the two product conventions and the shift/twist consistent. The first display contains an overwritten tensor/star, and the two formulas should be checked together without changing either.

After rearranging factors, the birigidified line N corresponds to ψ:C→B*, whose two components are asserted to equal the map induced by L. This reduces the inversion calculation to a universal direct-image problem; the next page must supply that computation.

The equal-components description of ψ suggests that its zero fibre is the anti-diagonal when the component is an isomorphism. That provides an internal way to test the symmetry appearing in the corrected theorem: track the support of the eventual composition kernel. This is a proposed consistency check based on the manuscript calculation, not a correction to its text.

The fibrewise vanishing lemma is used to place the support of the universal direct image on the unit section. This is a statement about support, not yet the claimed identification with the shifted determinant line pushed forward from that section. The rest of the page constructs the comparison morphism but does not yet prove it is an isomorphism.

The canonical comparison is chosen via the exterior algebra structure on the cohomology of O_B and the identification of R¹q_*O_B with the tangent space of the dual. This explains the determinant line τ_B* that appeared as a correction in the preceding pages. The last map is called the hom identique, fixing the intended normalization.

The proposed comparison is tested after derived pullback to points, with a reference to mapping cylinders. Off the unit section, the admitted vanishing lemma supplies the test. At the unit section, the proof reduces to a compatibility check over an algebraically closed field and leaves that check unwritten, ending in five dots.

The remarks record the exchange of translations/skyscraper-type classes with algebraically trivial line sheaves, and of convolution with tensoring by such a line sheaf. The signs and twists are revised repeatedly. One surviving product uses e_t while the immediately preceding images use e_{−t}; this is manuscript evidence that requires a convention check, not silent correction.

Applying the determinant after the transform is proposed to yield a map of relative Picard objects and then maps on components indexed by Néron–Severi sections. The compatibility assertion continues onto the next page. The visible minus sign on the target component is accompanied by a marginal double-negation calculation, signaling that signs are being actively tracked.

**Editorial confidence:** medium. The three test classes interact directly with the rank, translation and determinant identities on the page, while their expected transforms depend on normalization that remains to be checked.

The manuscript asks whether its Chern-character and total-Chern-class formulas hold modulo torsion. The equivalence relation and coefficient theory of that stronger question need to be fixed before comparing it with later work. The following paragraph asserts a weaker cohomological version, not an answer to this question.

The page connects the component map from the preceding leaf to a duality relation involving δ and δ′, with explicit negative signs. A later reconstruction should track the distinction between L′ and the determinant line L′⁻¹, since changing that convention would reverse the signs in all Chern expansions.

The manuscript uses Riemann–Roch for the addition morphism to relate convolution and the Chern character, with an explicit Todd factor from the tangent object t_A. The desired middle self-duality is identified with ampleness of a Néron–Severi class. This is the precise positivity claim that the previous page only begins to formulate, and it remains explicitly an unproved target.

In the Picard-family test case, expressD through the restriction/Gysin maps associated withY and identify its action on primitive cohomology. This would expose the sign and degeneracy issues flagged in the previous page’s margin before attempting positivity for arbitrary parameter spaces.

hits.section: ## Integral models, local duality, and reused typescripts
hits.text: The following items distinguish calculations made directly from the frozen pages from external comparisons made only after the transcription was frozen. Their conclusions are conditional wherever a normalization or an antecedent hypothesis is not supplied on the surviving sheet; no mathematical correction is inserted into the transcription.

hits.section: ### R2 — Own idea: contraction and the unweighted lowering operator
hits.text: Choose the contraction convention \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{std}}=\sum_j\iota_{f_j^\vee}\iota_{e_j^\vee}\) in the rank-four example of R1; then \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{std}}L(1)=2\), whereas the endpoint identity \(\Lambda L=1-\sum_{j\ge n}\pi_{j,0}\) acts as 1 on degree 0. Over a characteristic-zero field, a primitive vector of degree \(i\) in an ordinary Lefschetz string satisfies \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{std}}(L^j p)=j(n-i-j+1)L^{j-1}p\), while an unweighted inverse along the same string sends \(L^j p\) to \(L^{j-1}p\). These are different operators even after rationalizing the integral model, so rationalization by itself does not settle the identification made on scan 14. The precise definition of contraction and any normalization outside the supplied pages must be checked before attributing a finished theorem to this draft.

hits.section: ### R4 — Own idea: an explicit discriminant pairing
hits.text: Replacing \(x\) or \(y\) by a representative differing by a column combination of \(Q\) changes the value by an integer, and the dual-lattice description proves that this pairing is perfect. In the rank-one case \(Q=(-m)\), it becomes \(b_Q(\bar a,\bar b)=-ab/m\pmod{\mathbb Z}\) on \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\), making both the determinant and the sign convention visible. This supplies the linear-algebra part of the claim on the page; identifying the geometric Néron–Severi quotient with \(D_Q\) still depends on the preceding geometric hypotheses.
