hits.section: ### R7 — Reading question: the typed word “homogènes”
hits.text: The typescript visibly says “homogènes”, although no grading has been introduced on this surviving page. Reading it as a claim about principal or monogenic maximal ideals would be a mathematical emendation, and even that emendation would need a field-size qualification: in \(\mathbb F_2^3\), every maximal ideal is generated by an idempotent while the algebra is not monogenic, as in R6. The appropriate research task is to locate the referenced proposition and its hypotheses, then compare its terminology with the exact typed wording retained here.

hits.section: ### R8 — Own idea: separate torsion from the rational Brauer quotient
hits.text: Under the finiteness and divisibility hypotheses explicitly imposed on the page, tensoring (8.7) with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) identifies \(V_\ell\operatorname{Br}'(X)\) with the quotient of \(H^2(X,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\) by the image of \(\operatorname{NS}(X)\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\). If the cycle-class map has the stated injectivity and \(\operatorname{NS}(X)\) has rank \(\rho\), this gives the dimension calculation \(\dim V_\ell\operatorname{Br}'(X)=b_2-\rho\). Neither calculation recovers finite \(\ell\)-primary groups, so the torsion comparisons elsewhere in (8.3)–(8.7) remain separate information rather than consequences of the dimension formula. This is a useful check on what “transcendental part” means in this particular passage.

hits.section: ### R10 — Own idea: isolate the adjunction in the injective-sheaf argument
hits.text: Since taking a stalk is exact, the right side is exact contravariantly in \(F\), proving that \(i_{x*}I\) is injective among all \(\mathcal O_X\)-modules. For the particular injective hull \(I=E(k(\mathfrak p))\) used on the page, the distinct geometric step is the identification \(\widetilde I\simeq i_{x*}I\): the displayed filtration reduces it to modules annihilated by powers of \(\mathfrak p\), for which localization is zero when the inverted element belongs to \(\mathfrak p\) and is an isomorphism when it does not. This separates the general adjunction argument from the noetherian algebra needed to establish that identification.

hits.section: ### R16 — Unproved claim: trace duality needs its own assumptions
hits.text: The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

hits.section: ### R18 — Unproved claim: make the two boundedness arguments explicit
hits.text: For coherent cohomology, case (a) has a precise current counterpart: a bounded-above first argument and bounded-below second argument give coherent internal derived Hom on a locally noetherian scheme (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0D0C, Lemma 36.11.5). The essential proof obligation is convergence with only finitely many relevant terms in each total degree, followed by coherence of the ordinary Ext modules. In the finite-injective-dimension version of case (b), truncating the first argument reduces each fixed output degree to case (a), as in Tag 0G4H, Lemma 47.15.2; one must still justify how the page's uniform sheaf-Ext bound supplies the needed local truncation estimate. The quasi-coherent variant and the exact scope of that uniform bound should be checked separately rather than inferred from the coherent statement alone.

hits.text: is not finite-dimensional. Moreover \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_k(k,M)=k\) for all \(i\ge0\), so the extra uniform vanishing condition in (b) fails exactly where required. This gives a small explicit obstruction to deleting that condition, independently of the continuation missing from the supplied page.

hits.text: The page proposes ordinary multiplication by an alternating bivector and contraction by its dual as an integral model for the preceding Lefschetz identities, but its displayed construction does not specify divided powers or a change to normalized lowering. The separate editorial calculations R1–R2 exhibit the factorial obstruction to integral hard Lefschetz and distinguish contraction from unit-step lowering; they therefore prevent importing the matrix algebra in item S3 directly into the written \(\Phi_0=\mathbb Z[L_0,\Lambda_0]\). The accessible publisher record establishes that bibliographic identification, but the article's full text was not obtained in this research pass, so no additional theorem is attributed to it here. It does not alone determine the scheme-theoretic structure along that section, the surviving cohomological degree, the determinant twist, or the specific comparison map constructed at the bottom of the page.

hits.text: **Editorial distinction:** with the corrected \(c_k\), the coefficient asserted integral at the foot of the page equals \((-1)^k r\,c_k(E)\), rather than \(c_k(E)\) itself. hits.section: ### S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem
hits.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.
